--- layout: dilemma permalink: /dilemmas/care-ethics-dinner-at-six-thirty/ title: "Dinner at Six-Thirty Sharp" summary: "A housekeeper has cared for a family for many years, but one night they learn what the six-thirty dinner is for." ---

For many years, a housekeeper has kept a household running for a family. The housekeeper has come to know the family's routines, one of which is that dinner must be ready at six-thirty sharp, every night.

One night the housekeeper learns why the time matters so much. A child shares that dinner must be at six-thirty sharp so that they can make it to a "special meeting." The housekeeper asks what happens at the special meeting, at which point the child describes a Klan meeting.

Nothing about the relationship has changed, and the family still depends on the housekeeper. The housekeeper is still the person who knows best what the family needs.

What should be done? Does care ethics suggest the housekeeper should simply "keep making dinner on time"?

Source: Victoria Davion, "Autonomy, Integrity, and Care," Social Theory and Practice 19, no. 2 (1993): 161–182. Davion uses the example of a caregiver who does not know that the person "needs dinner at six-thirty sharp in order to make it to a Klan meeting."

Context: This example illustrates a common objection to care ethics related to "slave morality." Slave morality is Nietzsche's term for the way that oppressed groups can sometimes develop ethical approaches that reinforce their own oppression. A shallow reading of care ethics would justify the dinner, as long as the caring relationship itself is going well.

See also: Carol Gilligan, In a Different Voice: Psychological Theory and Women's Development

See also: Joan Tronto, Moral Boundaries: A Political Argument for an Ethic of Care (Routledge, 1993), and Virginia Held, The Ethics of Care: Personal, Political, and Global (Oxford University Press, 2006) — care ethicists answer this objection by arguing that care must be social, communal, and political, not just a matter of individual relationships.
